title: How to Love Your Enemy
excerpt: It is the command we admire from a safe distance and refuse to practice up close. Jesus did not mean love your enemy in theory. He meant the person you actually cannot stand.
body:
Jesus said love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, and we have spent two thousand years admiring the sentence while avoiding the person. It is easy to love an enemy who is far away and abstract. It is another thing entirely to love the coworker who undermined you, the relative whose cruelty still aches, the stranger online whose every post seems engineered to insult what you hold sacred. The command was never about the abstract enemy. It was about the one with a name.

We should be honest that this is the hardest thing in the faith. It cuts against every instinct of self-protection. And in our moment it has a new difficulty, because the wider culture has taught us to manufacture enemies by the millions out of people we have never met, sorting whole categories of human beings into the column marked threat. We did not invent this contempt. We absorbed it. And then we baptized it.

## The enemy is not an exception to neighbor love

We treat enemy love as an advanced module, a heroic extra for the spiritually gifted. Jesus treats it as the proof that your love is real at all. If you love those who love you, he said, what reward is that. Even the people you despise do that much. The love that testifies to something beyond ordinary human decency is the love that reaches the person who has wronged you. That is the whole point. Anyone can love a friend. Only grace can love an enemy.

Notice that Jesus does not redefine the enemy as secretly nice, or ask you to pretend the wrong did not happen. He keeps the word enemy. The person really did the thing. And you are still commanded to love. Love here is not a warm feeling you must gin up. It is a settled commitment to seek the good of someone you would rather see fail.

## Start with prayer, because it changes the one praying

The command comes with a method attached: pray for those who persecute you. This is not incidental. It is almost impossible to keep hating a person you are genuinely praying for, because prayer drags them out of the category enemy and back into the category human being made in God's image. You cannot ask God to bless someone every day and keep them flat in your mind as a cartoon villain. The praying does not change them. It changes you, slowly, into someone whose heart has stopped clenching at their name.

I have prayed through gritted teeth for people I did not want God to bless, and I will tell you the prayer felt like a lie at first. It was not a lie. It was a surgery. The asking, repeated, loosened a grip I did not know I was holding.

## Refuse the tribe's enemies list

Here is where our moment needs naming. The American argument hands every believer a ready-made enemies list, updated daily, sorted by party. One side is taught to despise a category of people, the other side a different category, and both call the contempt righteousness. A Christian who simply adopts his tribe's enemies has not thought about Jesus at all. He has let the party do his hating for him.

The ancient Christian ethic refuses this on principle. The early church was full of people who had been enemies to each other, zealot and tax collector, slave and free, Jew and Gentile, seated at one table because the cross had outranked their tribes. The gospel does not give you permission to hate the people your side hates. It takes your enemies list and burns it.

## Love is concrete, not sentimental

Paul makes enemy love embarrassingly practical. If your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him a drink. Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good. The love is a sandwich, a glass of water, an actual deed done for the good of a real person you would rather avoid. It is not a feeling you wait to arrive. It is a thing you do, and the feeling, if it comes, comes after.

This is why enemy love is possible even when it is not pleasant. You do not have to like someone to refuse to slander them, to decline the satisfying revenge, to wish them genuine good. Those are choices, available to you on the worst day, no warmth required.

## This week

Name one actual enemy. Not a category, not a party, a person with a face who has wronged you or whom you have learned to despise. Begin praying for that person by name, daily, asking God to bless them, even if the words feel false at first. Then do one concrete good for them or refuse one piece of contempt you would normally enjoy. Watch what happens to your own heart. The command was never going to come easy. It was always going to come.

title: How to Care for the Poor Without Condescension
excerpt: The poor do not need your pity, your savior complex, or your theory about why they are poor. They need to be treated as what they are, image-bearers owed dignity, not problems to be managed.
body:
There is a way of helping the poor that wounds them, and most of us have practiced it without meaning to. It treats the poor man as a project, the giver as a hero, and the gift as a transaction that leaves the giver feeling generous and the receiver feeling small. The help arrives, and so does a quiet message underneath it: I am above you, and you are a case I have decided to take on. The poor feel that message long after the food is eaten.

Proverbs says whoever oppresses the poor insults his Maker, and whoever is generous to the needy honors him. Note the standard. The poor man is not God's afterthought. He is, in some sense, God's proxy, made in his image, and to treat him with condescension is to insult the One whose likeness he bears. Dignity is not a nice addition to mercy. It is the heart of it.

## See a person, not a category

The first condescension is the one that happens before you give anything: reducing the poor to a type. The lazy poor, the noble poor, the deserving, the undeserving. Every tribe hands you a category that confirms what you already believe, and the category lets you keep your distance, because you never have to meet anyone. You just have to have an opinion.

Draw near, and the categories break. You meet a particular man with a particular story, and you discover the type fit almost no one you actually met. Caring for the poor without condescension begins by learning a name and listening to a story before you form a theory. The face dissolves the abstraction. You cannot patronize someone whose story you have actually heard.

## Kill the lie that you earned it

Condescension grows in the soil of a particular lie: that what you have is a wage you deserved rather than a gift you were given. If your comfort is earned, then their need is their failure, and your generosity is charity from above. But the law kept reminding Israel, you were slaves in Egypt, you did not earn your freedom, you were rescued. The line between you and the poor is not virtue. It is grace, an accident of birth, a kindness you did not arrange.

When that lands, the posture changes. You are not a benefactor stooping down. You are one beggar telling another where bread can be found. I have caught the savior complex in my own giving, the warm glow of being the helper, and the glow was the tell. Real mercy does not need to feel superior. It has already admitted it is the same.

## Work with people, not on them

The law of Moses did not just hand out food. It left the corners of the field unharvested so the poor could glean, working with their own hands on what the owner deliberately left. That is dignity built into the structure: not a handout that makes a man passive, but a margin that lets him labor and eat with his head up. The best help treats the poor as partners and agents, not objects to be processed.

This means asking before assuming, listening before fixing, and resisting the help that makes you feel good while leaving the person dependent and diminished. Sometimes the most dignifying thing is to receive from them, to eat their food, to let them host you, to be served. That levels the ground in a way no gift can.

## Refuse both tribes' scripts

The American argument will try to capture your mercy. One side will tell you the poor are victims to be pitied, which is its own condescension. The other will tell you the poor are mostly at fault, which is contempt with a budget attached. The ancient Christian ethic refuses both. It holds that the poor bear God's image and are owed dignity, and that they are agents responsible for their lives, and that calamity, injustice, and folly all put people in the ditch, and that none of this changes the command to love the actual neighbor in front of you. Do not let your party script your compassion.

## This week

Find one poor person and learn their name and story before you give them anything. Listen longer than is comfortable. Then help in a way that treats them as a partner, not a project, and that costs you something you will not announce. Check your own heart for the warm glow of the helper, and when you find it, remember Egypt. You were rescued too.

title: How to Engage Politics Without Losing Your Soul
excerpt: You can care about justice without making a kingdom of this world your god. The ancient creed that got Christians killed was political, and it set them free.
body:
Watch your body when the other side wins an election. The drop in the stomach, the dread that feels almost spiritual. Watch when your side wins: the surge of vindication, the sense that the country has been saved. Those are not the responses of a citizen casting a vote. They are the responses of a worshiper whose god has been threatened or enthroned. Most of us, if we are honest, recognize the feeling. And the feeling is the warning.

Something has happened to the believer, and it happened so gradually we did not feel it occur. Politics stopped being one arena of life and became the arena, the lens that sorts who our friends are, which Christians are sound, and whether the future is hope or catastrophe. We did not decide to make a kingdom of this world ultimate. We absorbed it the way you absorb a fever. And now a political identity sits where a religious one used to be, often wearing its clothes.

## The tell: the tribe now reads the Bible

Here is the symptom that should alarm us. For many believers, the tribe now reads the Bible instead of the Bible reading the tribe. You can tell, before a Christian opens his mouth on any subject, what he will say, because you already know how he votes. The politics has become the fixed thing, and the faith bends to fit it. Without quite noticing, we let the parties disciple us. They got there first, more present and more emotionally insistent than the slow voice of Scripture.

Losing your soul in politics does not look like a dramatic apostasy. It looks like excusing in your own side what you condemn in the other. It looks like receiving comfortable lies because they serve your team. It looks like contempt you have learned to feel righteous about.

## Render to Caesar, and not one inch more

When they tried to trap Jesus on taxes, he asked whose image was on the coin. Caesar's, they said. Then render to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's. The line is exact and devastating. Caesar gets his coin, his taxes, his real and limited authority. But the image on the coin is Caesar's, and the image on you is God's, and what bears God's image belongs to God alone. Caesar gets the coin. He does not get the worshiper.

This is the whole of political sanity. The state is real, ordained, owed honest engagement. The state is not ultimate, and the moment it asks for the allegiance that belongs to God, the Christian says no, the way the martyrs said no to the pinch of incense before Caesar's image. Polycarp died over that distinction. Engage politics, yes. But know where the coin ends and the worship begins.

## Hope makes you free

The gospel gives the believer a freedom no party can. Because your ultimate hope rests on a King already enthroned, you can engage with energy and without idolatry, with conviction and without despair. You can lose an election without losing your world, because your world was never up for a vote. You can love your opponent as a neighbor rather than hate him as an enemy, because your security does not depend on defeating him.

This is not apathy. Indifference is not the goal and detachment is not the gospel. It is the calm of a person who has read the end of the story and knows which kingdom stands. From that calm you can work hard for a just cause and still sleep, because the outcome rests in hands that were nailed for you and not in the hands of an electorate.

## Tell the truth to your own side

The deepest test of whether the faith owns the politics or the politics owns the faith is whether you can name the sins of your own tribe. The idolater excuses in his side what he condemns in the other, because the tribe is his god and a god can do no wrong. The believer set free can say the hard, costly word to the people whose approval he most wants, because he answers to a higher King than the crowd. It will get you called a traitor by your own. That is the price of having only one Lord.

## This week

Notice your body the next time the news breaks, and name the dread or the vindication honestly as worship rather than citizenship. Then do two things. Pray by name for a leader you did not vote for, that God would grant them wisdom. And say one true, costly thing about your own side's sins, out loud, to someone in it. Notice how hard the second one is. The difficulty is the measure of how much the tribe already owns.

title: How to Be a Faithful Citizen
excerpt: Scripture makes you a resident alien, a citizen of heaven who loves the country he does not worship. That is not a contradiction. It is the only way to be a citizen without becoming an idolater.
body:
The Bible gives the Christian a strange dual citizenship that the tribes keep collapsing into one. Paul says our citizenship is in heaven. Peter calls us sojourners and exiles, resident aliens whose deepest loyalty lies elsewhere. And the same Paul submits to the governing authorities, uses his Roman citizenship to demand justice, and tells us to pray for kings. The same prophets who relativize every nation command God's exiles in Babylon to seek the welfare of the city, to build houses and plant gardens and pray for the peace of a pagan empire.

So the faithful citizen is neither an anarchist nor a hermit. He is a resident alien who loves the country he does not worship, works for its good, prays for its rulers, tells it the truth, and serves his neighbor through its common life, precisely because his hope is not riding on it. Hold both halves and you have the only stable ground there is. Drop either one, and you have either withdrawal or idolatry.

## Seek the welfare of the city

God's word to the exiles in Babylon is the charter of faithful citizenship: seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you, and pray for it, for in its welfare you will find your welfare. Notice it is a pagan city, the very empire that carried them off, and they are told to work for its good anyway. This kills the idea that faithful citizenship means waiting for a Christian nation before you participate. You build, plant, and seek peace in the actual country you are in, flawed as it is.

This means showing up. Voting thoughtfully. Knowing your neighbors. Serving on the school board or the food bank or the jury. Telling the truth in public. The faithful citizen is present and useful, not because the nation is ultimate, but because his neighbors are real and the laws and structures shape their lives.

## Honor the authorities without worshiping them

Peter says honor the emperor, and he wrote it about an emperor who would later have Christians killed. Honoring authority is not the same as approving of it, and it is certainly not worshiping it. The Christian pays his taxes, obeys the just laws, prays for leaders he despises, and refuses the contempt that the culture treats as a civic virtue. Daniel served pagan kings with integrity and without flattery. Joseph administered an empire that was not his and did it honestly. You can give a government real honor while denying it the ultimate allegiance it keeps asking for.

And there is a limit, marked clearly. When the authorities command what God forbids, the apostles answered, we must obey God rather than men. Honor is real but not infinite. Caesar gets the coin. He does not get your conscience.

## Refuse the partisan capture of citizenship

The American argument will try to convince you that faithful citizenship means total enlistment in a party, that any Christian who will not fully enlist is naive or compromised. Both tribes make the same demand in opposite colors: give us your ultimate allegiance, let your hope and your fear be set by us. The ancient Christian ethic refuses this. A citizen of heaven cannot be wholly owned by any earthly faction, because his deepest belonging was purchased from every tribe and tongue.

This frees you to vote without idolatry and to disagree without despair. You can support a cause with conviction and still see its blind spots, because the party is not your god and its platform is not your scripture. The faithful citizen is the freest voter in the room, owned by no faction, terrified of no result.

## Tell the truth in public

The prophets engaged the public square mainly by telling it the truth, and they told it to kings who could kill them. Faithful citizenship includes a witness: naming injustice, defending the vulnerable, refusing the comfortable lie even when it serves your side. This is not the same as winning. It is bearing honest testimony in a country that increasingly rewards the lie that flatters the tribe. I have stayed silent when truth was costly and called it prudence. It was not prudence. It was fear, and the faithful citizen has to repent of it.

## This week

Do one concrete thing for the welfare of your actual city, with no partisan angle attached: serve a need, show up to a local meeting, help a neighbor through the common life of the place. Then pray, by name, for a leader you did not vote for, asking God to give them wisdom. You are a resident alien. Love the country. Do not worship it. The distinction is the whole of faithful citizenship.

title: How to Care for Creation as a Christian
excerpt: The first job God gave a human being was to tend a garden. Caring for creation is not a borrowed cause from the culture. It is the oldest assignment in the Bible.
body:
Before there was a temple, a law, or a single commandment about worship, there was a garden and a gardener. God put the man in Eden to work it and keep it, and the word translated keep is the same word used for guarding and protecting. The first vocation given to a human being was the care of a place. This is not a modern cause grafted onto the faith. It is in the opening pages, written into what a human being is for.

We have largely lost this, and we lost it for a reason worth naming. The moment creation care comes up, an alarm sounds, because the subject has been captured by the American argument, sorted into a partisan column, and most believers have decided it must therefore belong to the other side. We let a political fight tell us which parts of Genesis to ignore.

## The earth is the Lord's, not ours

The Psalmist says the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof. This single line dismantles two errors at once. Against the one who thinks the world is ours to use up however we please, it says the world belongs to God, not to us, and we are stewards who will give an account. Against the one who wants to worship the creation itself, it says the earth is the Lord's, his handiwork, to be honored as a gift and not adored as a god. The Christian neither plunders the world nor deifies it. He keeps it, as a trust from its Maker.

Dominion, the word God gave the man, has been badly abused to mean domination. But the dominion of God's image-bearer is meant to mirror God's own rule, which feeds the ravens, clothes the lilies, and notices the sparrow that falls. To have dominion the way God does is to care, to cultivate, to make a place flourish, not to strip it bare and walk away.

## Creation is not yours to exhaust

The law built rhythms of rest into the land itself. Every seventh year the fields were to lie fallow, the soil allowed to recover. This was not sentimentality. It was a structural refusal to treat the creation as an endless resource to be squeezed until it failed. The God of the law would not let his people exhaust the ground any more than he would let them exhaust the poor. Both bore his concern. Both had limits he commanded his people to honor.

This cuts against a way of living that treats consumption as limitless and consequence as someone else's problem. The Christian who believes the earth is the Lord's cannot be casual about wasting it, fouling it, or handing his children a depleted version of the gift he was given. Stewardship has a time horizon longer than my own convenience.

## Creation groans, and waits

Paul says the whole creation groans, subjected to futility, waiting for its redemption alongside the children of God. The Christian hope is not that the world will be discarded while souls float off to heaven. It is that creation itself will be renewed, that there will be a new heavens and a new earth. This matters enormously for how we treat the world now. If the material creation is destined for the trash, you can use it up. If it is destined for redemption, it is to be honored now as a thing God has not given up on.

That is why creation care is not a distraction from the gospel. It is a sign of it, a small foretaste of the day when all things are made new, lived out in advance by people who refuse to treat God's good world as disposable.

## Refuse the partisan frame

Here the partisan capture has to be named and refused directly. One tribe has made creation care a flag, and another has made denial of it a loyalty test, and the believer is told he must pick a team. The ancient Christian ethic predates both teams by millennia. It does not arrive at creation care through a party platform. It arrives through Genesis, the Psalms, the law, and Paul. Tend the garden because God told the first human to, not because a party told you to, and not refusing to tend it because a different party told you not to.

## This week

Pick one concrete, unglamorous act of keeping the garden, and do it as worship rather than politics. Waste less of something. Tend a piece of ground, a tree, a patch of land near you. Repair instead of replace. Refuse one habit of careless consumption you have justified because everyone does it. Do it quietly, as the oldest assignment in the Bible, given to a gardener in a garden long before there was a party to argue about it.

title: How to Handle Money in an Affluent Society
excerpt: Jesus said more about money than almost anything else, and almost none of it is comfortable for the comfortable. Handling money well begins by admitting how much it already handles you.
body:
Jesus talked about money constantly, and the comfortable have learned to read past it the way we read past the prophets on the poor. You cannot serve God and money, he said, naming wealth as a rival god with a will of its own, not a neutral tool. He told a rich young ruler to sell what he had. He warned that it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom. He told a story about a man who built bigger barns and died the night he finished. The pattern is unmistakable, and it is aimed straight at us, because by the measure of history and the world, we are the rich young ruler.

The first honest move is to admit that money is not just sitting in your account. It is shaping your fears, your sense of security, your status, and your sleep. In an affluent society, the danger is not that we will worship a golden calf in the open. It is that we will worship comfort quietly, while calling it responsibility.

## Name money as a rival, not a neutral

Jesus personifies wealth on purpose. Mammon is a master, and it competes for the seat that God alone should hold. The reason the comfortable rarely feel the danger is that the idol of money does not announce itself. It works through reasonable-sounding things: planning, security, providing, getting ahead. None of those are evil. But underneath them can run a quiet trust that says, if I have enough, I am safe, which is a confession that your real security is in the account and not in God.

The test is simple and uncomfortable. What threatens your peace most? For many of us it is not the state of our soul but the state of our finances, and that ranking tells you which master is actually in charge.

## Generosity is the lever that breaks money's grip

Jesus prescribes a specific medicine for the love of money, and it is not guilt. It is giving. Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also, he said, and the order matters. Move the treasure and the heart follows. You do not become free from money's grip by feeling bad about wealth. You become free by giving it away, regularly and sacrificially, until the open hand is simply the shape of how you live.

This is why the early church gave so radically that, Luke says, there was not a needy person among them. They had discovered that generosity is not a tax on the rich but a rescue for the rich, a way of loosening a grip that would otherwise harden the heart. Give first, before life bends the giving down. Give enough to feel it. And give in secret, so the giving works on your heart and not your reputation.

## Refuse both tribes' money gospels

The affluent society offers two false gospels of money, and the church has baptized both. One says that wealth is a sign of God's favor and your own virtue, that prosperity is the reward of the faithful. That is a lie the prophets would have torched. The other says that money is dirty and the spiritual person despises it and the system that produces it. That is its own kind of pride, often held by people quite comfortable. The ancient Christian ethic refuses both. It says wealth is a gift and a danger, that the rich are not heroes and not villains but stewards under judgment, and that the question is never how much you have but whose you are and whose it is.

Do not let a party tell you whether your money is a trophy or a crime. Let Scripture tell you it is a trust, on loan, to be handled with open hands and a sober heart.

## Contentment is the quiet rebellion

Paul learned the secret of being content in plenty and in want, and called it a secret because the affluent society works tirelessly to keep us from it. The whole machine runs on discontent, on the conviction that you need the next thing to be complete. Contentment is the quiet rebellion against that machine. Godliness with contentment, Paul says, is great gain. The person who has learned to say enough has escaped a treadmill that most of the rich will run until they die.

I have run that treadmill, telling myself the next acquisition was the responsible one. It never was the last one. The treadmill does not have a last one. Only contentment gets you off it.

## This week

Look honestly at what threatens your peace most, and ask whether money has taken a seat that belongs to God. Then do one concrete thing to loosen its grip: give something away that you will actually feel, in secret, this week. And practice one act of contentment, refusing one purchase the machine has convinced you that you need. Move the treasure, and watch the heart begin, slowly, to follow.

title: How to Seek the Good of Your City
excerpt: God told his exiles to seek the welfare of the very city that had carried them off. Your city is not a backdrop to your real life. It is the place God has sent you to bless.
body:
When God's people were dragged into exile in Babylon, they expected a word of resistance or a promise of quick escape. Instead the prophet Jeremiah brought them a stranger command: build houses and live in them, plant gardens and eat what they produce, seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you, and pray to the Lord on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare. The city was pagan. It was the enemy. And they were told to seek its good as if it were their own.

That command is the charter for how a Christian relates to the place he lives. Your city, your town, your neighborhood, is not a backdrop to your real life somewhere else. It is the place God has sent you, and you are to seek its flourishing, not just tolerate it while waiting to leave.

## Your welfare is bound to its welfare

The logic Jeremiah gives is the part we resist. In the welfare of the city you will find your welfare. The exiles wanted to keep their good separate from Babylon's, to thrive while the city around them failed. God ties the two together. The Christian does not flourish in a bubble while his city decays. He is woven into the place, and its health and his are bound together. This kills the suburban fantasy of a private life sealed off from the troubles of the place you live.

This means caring about your city's actual problems: its schools, its lonely, its poor, its broken families, its tired institutions. Not as a project for the deserving few, but as the welfare of the place God planted you, which is now your welfare too.

## Build and plant, do not just consume

Notice the verbs. Build houses. Plant gardens. These are the actions of people who invest in a place for the long haul, not tourists passing through. Most of us consume our cities. We extract what we want, the job, the conveniences, the amenities, and contribute as little as possible, treating the place as a service provider rather than a community we belong to. Seeking the good of your city means becoming a builder and a planter, someone who puts more in than he takes out.

This is slow, unglamorous work. It looks like committing to a neighborhood and staying. Knowing the people. Joining the institutions that hold a place together and giving them your time. Starting the thing that needed starting. A city is blessed by people who decided to stay and build, not by people forever poised to leave.

## Pray for the place, by name

Jeremiah does not just say work for the city. He says pray for it. There is something the prayer does that the work alone cannot. It changes how you see the place. It is hard to keep despising a city you are genuinely praying for, hard to keep treating it as a problem when you are carrying it before God. Pray for your city by name, its leaders, its needy, its specific wounds, and watch your heart soften toward a place you may have been quietly looking down on.

The early church did this in cities far more hostile than ours. They stayed during plagues when those with means fled. They took in the abandoned. They prayed for an empire that persecuted them. And the cities noticed, and many of them were won, not by argument but by people who plainly loved the place.

## Refuse the partisan map of your city

The American argument hands you a map of your city sorted into us and them, the right kind of neighborhood and the wrong kind, the people who belong and the people who are a problem. The ancient Christian ethic refuses that map. The welfare you are to seek is the welfare of the whole city, including the parts and the people your tribe has written off. Babylon was not a sympathetic city. They were told to seek its good anyway. You do not get to seek the welfare only of the neighbors who vote like you. The command is for the whole place.

## This week

Pick one concrete way to put more into your city than you take out, and do it: serve a need, join an institution that holds the place together, help a neighbor through the common life of the city. Then begin praying for your city by name, including the parts of it you have been tempted to despise. You are not just passing through. God sent you here. Seek the welfare of the place, and you will find, strangely, your own.

title: How to Disagree About Politics With People You Love
excerpt: We are losing marriages, friendships, and family over elections, at a rate our grandparents would not recognize. Here is how to keep your convictions and keep your people.
body:
Something has gone wrong when a family stops speaking over a vote, when a friendship of decades ends over a candidate, when a holiday table becomes a theater of war. We are losing the people we love over politics at a rate that would have baffled our grandparents, who managed to disagree about elections and still pass the potatoes. The wider culture has taught us that those who differ politically are not merely wrong but dangerous, and we have let that lesson into our homes.

Christians have caught the same disease, and it is killing our witness, because a faith that cannot stay in the room with people who disagree has nothing to offer a divided world. Jesus kept company with a zealot who wanted Rome overthrown and a tax collector who collaborated with Rome, at the same table, in the same band of disciples. He loved them into a room together. That is the model, and it is harder than picking a side.

## Decide the relationship outranks the argument

The decisive move happens before the conversation: this person matters more to me than winning this point. If you have not settled that in advance, the heat of the moment will settle it for you, and you will choose the win and lose the person. Most political arguments are not actually about policy. They are about whether each person feels respected and whether each one feels safe. Decide that the people you love will leave the conversation feeling loved even if neither of you moved an inch, and you have already kept what matters.

This is not cowardice and it is not mushiness. It is the refusal to sacrifice a real human being on the altar of a point you could have made another way, or never needed to make at all.

## Find the fear or the value underneath

Underneath almost every political position is a fear or a wound or a value worth honoring. The relative whose politics alarm you is usually protecting something they love, a way of life, a vulnerable group, a moral order they fear is collapsing. Ask why they hold what they hold, and listen for the thing underneath. Proverbs says to answer before listening is folly and shame, and most of our political arguments are folly and shame by that definition, because we are loading the rebuttal while they are still talking.

Try stating their view back so well that they say, yes, that is what I mean. The person who feels truly understood can tolerate disagreement. The person who feels caricatured cannot, and most of our family fights are fights between two caricatures, neither of which anyone actually holds.

## Hold conviction, refuse contempt

You can hold a political conviction firmly and refuse contempt entirely. The culture insists these are the same thing. They are not. To disagree is to think someone is wrong. To hold them in contempt is to think they are beneath you, stupid or evil for disagreeing. The first is honest. The second is poison, and the people you love feel it through every polite word. I have caught contempt in my own voice while saying all the reasonable things, and the contempt is what my people heard, not the reasonableness. Repent of the contempt and the disagreement can stay in the room without ending the relationship.

## Remember neither party is your church

Here the partisan capture must be named. The reason political disagreement now feels like a rupture in a family is that politics has become an identity, almost a religion, and to differ feels like a betrayal of the tribe. The ancient Christian ethic refuses to let either party become the thing that defines belonging. Your brother who votes differently is still your brother. Your friend across the line is still your friend. Their party is not their soul, and yours is not yours. When the baptism is thicker than the ballot, you can disagree about an election and still be one family, which is exactly the witness a sorted and bitter country is quietly desperate to see.

## This week

Think of one relationship currently strained by political disagreement, and take a step toward that person that has nothing to do with the argument: a call, a meal, a kind word that says you matter more to me than this. If the topic comes up, practice stating their view back until they agree you have understood it, before you say a word in reply. And listen for your own contempt. If you find it, set it down. You can keep your convictions. Do not lose your people to them.

title: How to Resist Consumerism
excerpt: The whole machine runs on convincing you that you are not yet complete. Resisting it is not about hating things. It is about refusing to let things tell you who you are.
body:
Consumerism is not the simple fact that we buy things. It is a story the surrounding world tells about who you are and how you become whole, and the story is this: you are incomplete, and the next purchase will complete you. The machine runs on discontent, manufactured and renewed daily, because a satisfied person buys less. You have been catechized by that story since before you could read, and the catechism is so constant you have stopped hearing it as a claim at all. You just feel the lack it created.

Jesus named the trap directly. A man's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions, he said, after a man asked him to settle an inheritance dispute. The whole consumer story is a denial of that sentence. It insists your life does consist in your possessions, that you are what you own, that the way to a full life runs through the checkout. Resisting consumerism begins by recognizing it as a rival gospel and not a neutral way of shopping.

## Name the lie of the next thing

The engine of consumerism is the lie of the next thing. Not this purchase, the next one, the one just out of reach, which will finally be enough. But the next thing, once acquired, immediately becomes the old thing, and a new next thing appears on the horizon, and the gap is never closed because the gap is the product. The machine is not selling you objects. It is selling you a permanent dissatisfaction that only it can briefly relieve, for a price, again and again.

Once you see it, you can start to refuse it. When you feel the pull toward a purchase, ask what it is really promising. Completeness? Status? Belonging? Relief from a feeling? Almost always the object is standing in for something it cannot deliver, and naming the real promise breaks part of its spell.

## Contentment is the counter-weapon

Paul says he learned the secret of being content in plenty and in want, and called it a secret because the consumer machine works tirelessly to keep us from it. Godliness with contentment, he writes, is great gain, and he sets it against the love of money that has plunged so many into ruin. Contentment is not resignation. It is the hard-won freedom of a person who has learned to say enough, which is the one word the entire machine is built to prevent you from saying.

This is learned, not felt. You practice enough until you mean it: a meal that does not need to be photographed, a wardrobe that does not need refreshing, a phone kept until it breaks. Each small act of enough is a deposit in a freedom the advertisers cannot reach.

## Generosity reverses the flow

Consumerism trains the hand to close and pull inward. Generosity is the deliberate reversal, the hand opening and pushing outward, and it does something to the heart that mere restraint cannot. Where your treasure is, Jesus said, there your heart will be also. Give things away, regularly and in secret, and you discover that you are less owned by them than you feared. The early church held their possessions loosely enough that there was not a needy person among them, and that loose grip was not poverty. It was freedom from the very thing that has us by the throat.

I have spent more energy acquiring than giving, and I have felt what it does, the slow tightening, the low anxiety of having things to protect. Generosity loosened it when nothing else could.

## Refuse the partisan misdirection

There is a partisan capture here too, and it deserves to be named. One political story treats consumption as the engine of the good life, growth and acquisition as nearly sacred. Another treats consumption as the great sin and turns its critique into a posture of superiority, often while consuming comfortably. The ancient Christian ethic predates and outranks both. It does not resist consumerism to score a point against a party. It resists because a man's life does not consist in his possessions, because the heart was made for God and will be restless until it rests in him, and no party owns that diagnosis. Do not let the critique of consumerism become its own form of pride or its own tribal flag.

## This week

Find the next purchase the machine has convinced you that you need, and refuse it, on purpose, and sit with the discomfort long enough to feel the manufactured lack for what it is. Then practice one act of enough and one act of generosity: keep something you would have replaced, and give something away in secret. You are not what you own. The machine has spent your whole life telling you otherwise. Start, in small repeated refusals, to stop believing it.

title: How to Use Technology Without Being Used by It
excerpt: Your devices are not neutral tools waiting for your intentions. They are designed to capture your attention and sell it. Using them well begins by admitting they are using you.
body:
We tell ourselves that technology is a neutral tool, that what matters is how you use it, that the device is just a hammer and the user decides whether to build or to break. This is a comforting lie. The hammer does not want anything. Your phone does. It was engineered by some of the most capable people alive to capture and hold your attention as long as possible, because your attention is the product being sold. To call that a neutral tool is to misunderstand both the tool and yourself.

Jesus said where your treasure is, your heart will be also, and we could update it without distortion: where your attention goes, your heart follows. The technologies that harvest your attention are therefore not just consuming your time. They are forming your heart, training your desires, shaping what you notice and what you crave. Using technology well begins by dropping the fiction that you are simply in charge.

## Admit the tool is shaping you

The first honest move is to admit the device is not passive. It is designed to pull you back, to interrupt, to make the next scroll more compelling than the last, to leave you slightly anxious and reaching for it again. This is not an accident or a side effect. It is the business model. The platforms profit precisely to the degree that they capture your attention, which means their incentive is your distraction, and a tool whose maker profits from your distraction is not a tool you can use casually.

Notice the evidence in your own life. The reflexive reach for the phone in the empty moment. The hour gone you cannot account for. The difficulty sitting still without a screen. These are not personal failures of willpower. They are the designed result, working exactly as intended, and naming it that way is the start of resistance.

## Attention is the soul's currency

The deep stakes are spiritual, because attention is the soul's currency. You become what you behold. The person who gives his attention all day to outrage becomes outraged. The one who gives it to comparison becomes envious and small. The one who gives it to noise loses the capacity for the silence in which God is usually heard. Be still and know that I am God, the Psalm says, and the technologies are engineered to make stillness nearly impossible. A heart that cannot be still cannot easily know God.

This is why the question is not only how much time you spend but what the spending is doing to you. A formed attention is a formed soul. An attention scattered and harvested all day is a soul scattered and harvested, no matter how orthodox your beliefs remain on paper.

## Build structures, not just intentions

Willpower loses to design. You will not out-discipline a system built by experts to defeat your discipline. What works is structure, decisions made once that remove the moment-by-moment fight. The phone out of the bedroom. The notifications off. The hours and the rooms where the device does not come. A sabbath from the screen. The early monastics ordered their days with rules and rhythms precisely because they knew the unguarded heart drifts, and you need the same: not a vague intention to use technology less, but a structure that decides for you when your willpower is gone.

The goal is not to flee technology into some imagined purity. It is to use it deliberately, as a servant, inside boundaries you set when you were clear-headed, rather than letting it use you in the moments when you are not.

## Refuse the partisan outrage machine

Here the partisan capture is especially sharp, because the most attention-harvesting content online is political outrage, and both tribes have learned to manufacture it. The machine does not care which side you are on. It profits from your fury either way, and it will feed you exactly the outrage your tribe craves to keep you scrolling. The ancient Christian ethic refuses this. It will not let the algorithm disciple your loves or set your enemies for you. Be slow to anger, James says, for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God, and the outrage machine produces nothing else. Refusing to be radicalized by your feed is now a spiritual discipline.

## This week

Build one structure, decided once, that takes the device out of a moment where it owns you: phone out of the bedroom, notifications off, one screen-free room or hour or day. Do not rely on willpower. Rely on the structure. Then notice what your attention has been doing to your heart, especially the outrage you have been fed, and starve it. You become what you behold. Behold something better than the thing engineered to harvest you.

title: How to Hold Justice and Mercy Together
excerpt: The tribes each keep half and call it the whole. Scripture refuses to let you choose between justice and mercy, because God never did.
body:
The prophet Micah reduces the whole duty of a human being to three things: do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God. He puts justice and mercy side by side, in one breath, as if they were obviously meant to be held together. And then we spend our lives prying them apart, each of us keeping the half our tribe prefers and treating the other half as the enemy's slogan.

One instinct says justice, meaning accountability, consequence, the righting of wrongs, the protection of order. The other says mercy, meaning compassion, forgiveness, the second chance, the binding of wounds. Each tribe holds its half so tightly that the other half starts to sound dangerous. But Scripture will not let you choose. At the cross, justice and mercy met and neither was sacrificed, and that meeting is the pattern the believer is called to live.

## God refuses to choose, and so must we

When God describes himself to Moses, he says he is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity, and that he will by no means clear the guilty. In one self-description he holds boundless mercy and uncompromising justice, and he does not seem to feel the tension we feel. He is not torn between them. They are both expressions of one holy character. The God who hears the cry of the oppressed and judges the oppressor is the same God who is patient, forgiving, and slow to wrath.

This means the believer who keeps only mercy and the believer who keeps only justice are each missing something essential about God himself. A mercy with no justice is sentimentality that lets evil roll on. A justice with no mercy is cruelty wearing a robe. God is neither, and his people are not allowed to be either.

## The cross holds both at full strength

The place where justice and mercy meet without either being diminished is the cross. There, God does not wink at evil to be merciful, and he does not crush the sinner to be just. He bears the justice himself so that mercy can be given freely. Paul says God did this to show that he is both just and the one who justifies, righteous and the giver of grace, in the same act. If you want to know whether justice and mercy can be held together at full strength, the answer is hanging on a Roman cross, and it cost everything.

This is why Christians cannot treat the two as rivals. We worship a God who refused to spare one for the other. The whole gospel is the holding together of what we keep tearing apart.

## In practice, both, toward the same person

Holding them together is not a slogan. It is a practice that meets you in particular situations. The wrongdoer in your life is owed both: the truth about what they did, named honestly, and the open door of mercy, held out genuinely. The poor man is owed both: compassion for his need and the dignity of being treated as a responsible agent, not a pet cause. The criminal, the addict, the betrayer, the broken: each is owed a love that neither excuses the wrong nor abandons the person. That is hard, far harder than keeping one half. It requires holding two things that pull against each other and refusing to drop either.

I find it easier to be merciful to people far away and just toward people who hurt me, which is exactly backward, and reveals that I am usually keeping whichever half is cheaper in the moment.

## Refuse the partisan division of the spoils

Here the partisan capture must be named clearly, because the two tribes have literally divided justice and mercy between them and each treats the other half as the enemy's property. One side claims justice and hears mercy as weakness. The other claims mercy and hears justice as cruelty. A Christian who simply picks up his tribe's half has let a political war amputate his theology. The ancient Christian ethic predates this division and refuses it. It will not surrender justice to one party or mercy to the other. It insists, with Micah, that the same person does justice and loves mercy, because the God he serves does both and divided them between no one.

## This week

Take one situation where you have been keeping only half, justice without mercy or mercy without justice, and ask what the missing half requires. Toward the person who wronged you, hold the truth and the open door together. Toward the cause you care about, hold compassion and accountability together. Refuse the partisan amputation that hands you one half and calls the other half the enemy's. Walk humbly, do justice, and love mercy, in the same breath, the way the God you serve always has.

title: How to Be In the World But Not Of It
excerpt: Jesus prayed that we would stay in the world without belonging to it. We keep failing in both directions, fleeing the world or being absorbed by it. There is a third way, and he prayed for it.
body:
On the night before he died, Jesus prayed for his followers, and the prayer holds a tension we keep collapsing. I do not ask that you take them out of the world, he said, but that you keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. In the world, not of it. Sent into it, not belonging to it. He prayed for that exact, difficult posture, and we keep failing in one direction or the other.

The two failures are familiar. One is to be of the world but barely in it, absorbed so completely into the surrounding culture that there is nothing distinct left, a Christian indistinguishable from anyone else. The other is to be against the world and out of it, retreating into a defensive enclave, hiding from the very people Jesus sent us to love. Both betray the prayer. The first dissolves the salt. The second buries it.

## Sent, not sealed off

Jesus says, as you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world. The Christian is not a refugee from the world but a missionary into it, placed deliberately among people who do not share the faith. The instinct to withdraw, to build a Christian bubble with Christian everything and only Christian friends, is a refusal of the sending. You cannot be salt in a saltshaker or light under a basket. The world Jesus sent you into includes the coworker, the neighbor, the relative, the stranger, all the people a sealed-off Christian never has to love.

This means presence, real and sustained, among people unlike you. Eating at their tables. Knowing their names. Being genuinely in the world, exposed to it, available to it, the way Jesus was constantly accused of being too close to the wrong people. The accusation that he was a friend of sinners was meant as an insult. It was actually the job description.

## Not of it, meaning your loves are different

But in the world is only half the prayer. Not of it is the other half, and it means your deepest loves, loyalties, and fears are set by a different kingdom. The world runs on certain engines, the love of money, the lust for status, the worship of comfort, the contempt for enemies, the manufacture of discontent. To be not of the world is to be visibly free of those engines, formed by something else, so that your life cannot quite be explained by the ordinary motives around you.

The early church grew in a hostile empire not mainly by argument but by this strange un-belonging. They took in abandoned babies, stayed in plague-stricken cities, forgave, shared, and refused to worship the emperor. They were thoroughly in the world and unmistakably not of it, and the not-of-it is what made people ask. A church identical to its culture has nothing to make anyone ask.

## The danger is being conformed without noticing

Paul commands, do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Conformity is the default, and it happens without a decision. You are formed by whatever you are soaked in, and most of us are soaked in the world's loves far more than the kingdom's, marinating in the same media, the same ambitions, the same outrages as everyone else, while assuming our beliefs keep us separate. They do not. Your loves are shaped by your habits, not your opinions, and a Christian conformed in his habits is of the world no matter what he affirms on Sunday.

This is the quiet failure. Not a dramatic apostasy but a slow conforming, until the believer wants the same things, fears the same things, and hates the same people as the world around him, with a religious vocabulary laid over the top.

## Refuse the partisan version of worldliness

Here the partisan capture must be named, because each tribe defines worldliness as the other tribe's sins. One side sees being of the world entirely in personal vice and never in the love of money or contempt for the poor. The other sees it entirely in injustice and never in the abandonment of holiness. Both edit the list to indict the enemy and excuse the self. The ancient Christian ethic refuses the partisan edit. Worldliness is the whole catalog of the world's disordered loves, and it lives in your tribe as surely as the other one. To be not of the world is to refuse conformity to all of it, including the conformity your own side calls righteousness.

## This week

Do two things that hold the prayer together. First, be more in the world: take one real step toward a person outside your Christian circle, a meal, a conversation, genuine presence among people who do not share your faith. Second, be more not of it: name one love or fear or contempt you have absorbed from the world, including from your own tribe, and refuse it deliberately. In the world, not of it. Jesus prayed it for you the night before he died. Live toward both halves, and drop neither.
